well-being = a state of being healthy, comfortable and content, not only free from illness
quality of life = how good or bad a person’s life feels in health, comfort and opportunity
life expectancy = the average number of years a person in a group is expected to live
public health = organised efforts to protect and improve the health of a whole population
health literacy = the ability to find, understand and use information to make health decisions
health inequality = unfair differences in health between social or economic groups
preventive care = medical services that stop illness before it starts or catches it early
risk factor = something that raises the chance of developing a disease
underlying condition = an existing long-term illness that makes other problems more serious
immune system = the body’s defences against infection
health promotion = activity that encourages people to live in ways that protect their health
screening programme = organised tests offered to a group to find disease early
early detection = finding a disease at a stage when treatment works better
preventable disease = an illness that vaccination, hygiene or lifestyle change can stop
universal healthcare = a system in which everyone can get medical care, usually paid from taxes
private healthcare = medical care paid for by the patient or a private insurer, not the state
medical ethics = moral rules that guide doctors, such as doing no harm and respecting choice
informed consent = agreement to treatment after the risks and benefits have been explained
patient confidentiality = the duty to keep a patient’s medical information private
chronic illness = a disease that lasts a long time and often cannot be fully cured
acute illness = an illness that starts suddenly and is often severe but may be short
infectious disease = an illness caused by bacteria, viruses or other microbes that can spread
non-communicable disease = a long-term illness that is not passed from person to person, such as diabetes
contagious = able to spread from one person to another
outbreak = a sudden rise in cases of a disease in a place or group
epidemic = when a disease spreads quickly to many people in a region
pandemic = an epidemic that spreads across many countries or the whole world
immunity = the body’s ability to resist a particular infection
herd immunity = protection that appears when enough people in a group are immune
antibody = a protein the body makes to recognise and fight a specific germ
vaccination = giving a vaccine to protect someone from a disease
booster dose = an extra vaccine given later to strengthen protection
vaccine hesitancy = delay or refusal of a vaccine despite it being available
immunisation = the process of becoming protected against a disease, usually by vaccine
quarantine = keeping people who may be infected away from others for a set time
self-isolation = staying at home and away from others because you are ill or at risk
inflammation = the body’s painful, red or swollen reaction to injury or infection
autoimmune disease = an illness in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissue
cardiovascular disease = illness of the heart and blood vessels
respiratory disease = illness of the lungs and airways
heart attack = a sudden blockage of blood to part of the heart muscle
stroke = a sudden loss of brain function because blood supply is blocked or a vessel bursts
hypertension = blood pressure that stays too high and damages organs over time
type 2 diabetes = a long-term condition in which the body cannot use insulin properly
tumour = an abnormal lump of cells that may be benign or malignant
cancer treatment = medical care such as surgery, drugs or radiotherapy used against cancer
terminal illness = a disease that cannot be cured and will lead to death
remission = a period when signs of a disease have reduced or disappeared
relapse = the return of an illness after a period of improvement
complication = an extra medical problem that appears because of a disease or treatment
prognosis = a doctor’s judgement of how an illness is likely to develop
diagnosis = the identification of an illness after tests and examination
fracture = a crack or break in a bone
traumatic brain injury = damage to the brain caused by a blow, jolt or penetrating wound
chronic pain = pain that lasts for months and often needs a mix of treatments
occupational disease = an illness caused by conditions at work, such as dust or chemicals
anaphylaxis = a sudden, life-threatening allergic reaction
antibiotic resistance = when bacteria survive drugs that used to kill them
sexually transmitted infection = an infection passed through sexual contact
antibiotic = a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing
prescription = a written order from a doctor for a medicine
generic drug = a medicine with the same active ingredient as a brand-name product, usually cheaper
over-the-counter medicine = a drug you can buy without a doctor’s order
recommended dose = the amount of a medicine that should be taken at one time
side effect = an unwanted result of a medicine or treatment
clinical trial = a carefully controlled test of a new treatment in people
placebo = a dummy treatment with no active drug, used to test whether a medicine really works
surgery = a medical operation that involves cutting or repairing the body
keyhole surgery = an operation done through small cuts, often with a camera
organ transplant = an operation that replaces a failing organ with one from a donor
organ donor = a person who gives an organ for transplant, in life or after death
blood transfusion = putting donated blood into a patient’s vein
physiotherapy = treatment that uses movement, exercise and massage to restore function
occupational therapy = treatment that helps people manage daily tasks after illness or disability
alternative medicine = treatments outside standard scientific medicine, such as some herbal or needle therapies
acupuncture = a therapy that uses thin needles at specific points on the body
medical rehabilitation = a programme of therapy to regain strength or skills after illness or injury
palliative care = care that relieves pain and stress when a disease cannot be cured
hospice = a place or service that cares for people with a terminal illness
pain management = planned medical help to reduce long-term or severe pain
treatment plan = an agreed set of steps for how a patient will be treated
follow-up appointment = a later visit to check how treatment is working
medical history = a record of past illnesses, operations, allergies and medicines
anaesthetic = a drug that stops you feeling pain during a procedure
MRI scan = a detailed image of the inside of the body made with magnets, not X-rays
operating theatre = the hospital room where surgeons perform operations
biopsy = removal of a small piece of tissue so it can be tested
GP = a general doctor you visit first, not a hospital specialist
the NHS = the United Kingdom’s publicly funded health service
A&E = the hospital department for sudden serious illness or injury
waiting list = a list of patients who must wait for a test, operation or specialist
health insurance = a policy that pays some or all of your medical costs
GP surgery = the clinic where a general practitioner sees patients
referral = a written request from a GP for you to see a specialist
consultant = a senior hospital specialist who leads a patient’s hospital care
outpatient = a patient who visits hospital for treatment but does not stay overnight
inpatient = a patient who stays in hospital overnight or longer
discharge = official permission to leave hospital after treatment
medical records = the written or digital file of a patient’s history and treatment
second opinion = advice from another doctor about a diagnosis or treatment
healthcare system = the organised network of hospitals, clinics, staff and funding in a country
primary care = first-contact health services, especially GPs, dentists and pharmacies
secondary care = hospital and specialist services after a GP referral
paramedic = a trained emergency clinician who treats people at the scene and in an ambulance
midwife = a specialist who cares for women during pregnancy, birth and after
paediatrician = a doctor who specialises in the health of babies and children
anaesthetist = a doctor who gives anaesthetics and watches the patient during surgery
pharmacist = a professional who prepares and advises on medicines
telemedicine = medical consultation by phone or video instead of a face-to-face visit
walk-in centre = a clinic you can attend without booking in advance
out-of-hours service = medical help available when the usual GP surgery is closed
medical negligence = harm caused when care falls below the standard a patient should expect
mental health = the condition of your mind and emotions, including how you cope with life
anxiety disorder = a mental-health condition with intense, lasting worry that disrupts daily life
counselling = talking regularly with a trained person to work through emotional problems
stigma = unfair shame or discrimination attached to an illness or situation
depression = a mental illness with lasting low mood, loss of interest and often poor sleep
bipolar disorder = a condition with extreme swings between high and low mood
anorexia nervosa = an eating disorder involving severe food restriction and a distorted body image
post-traumatic stress disorder = a condition after a shocking event, with flashbacks, nightmares and high alertness
emotional exhaustion = a state of feeling drained and unable to cope after prolonged stress
talking therapy = treatment that uses structured conversation rather than only medicine
cognitive behavioural therapy = a talking treatment that helps people change unhelpful thoughts and habits
psychiatrist = a medical doctor who diagnoses mental illness and can prescribe medicine
psychologist = a specialist in behaviour and the mind who offers assessment and therapy but is not a medical doctor
counsellor = a trained person who listens and helps you talk through problems
panic attack = a sudden episode of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heart
insomnia = a lasting difficulty falling or staying asleep
coping strategy = a method you use to manage stress or difficult emotions
support group = people with a similar problem who meet to share experience and encouragement
self-harm = hurting yourself on purpose as a way of dealing with emotional pain
mental-health crisis = a point when a person cannot stay safe or cope and needs urgent help
addiction = a condition in which you cannot control a harmful habit even when you want to stop
substance abuse = harmful or risky use of alcohol, drugs or other substances
alcoholism = addiction to alcohol that damages health, work or relationships
nicotine addiction = physical and psychological dependence on nicotine from tobacco or vapes
withdrawal symptoms = unpleasant physical or mental effects when a dependent person stops a substance
harm reduction = policies that lower the damage of drug use even if the person is not yet abstinent
binge drinking = drinking a large amount of alcohol in a short time
passive smoking = breathing in other people’s tobacco smoke
vaping = inhaling vapour from an electronic cigarette
gambling addiction = an inability to control betting despite serious harm
rehab clinic = a centre that treats people for addiction, often with therapy and medical support
addictive substance = a drug or chemical that can create dependence
healthy lifestyle = habits such as balanced eating, activity, sleep and avoiding harmful substances
sedentary lifestyle = a way of living with little physical movement
childhood obesity = a level of body fat in children that is high enough to harm present and future health
undernutrition = poor health caused by too little food, or food that lacks essential nutrients
sleep deprivation = a lasting lack of enough sleep
mindfulness = paying attention to the present moment, often used to reduce stress
physical inactivity = not doing enough movement to protect health
disability = a physical, sensory, intellectual or mental condition that makes some activities harder
accessibility = how easily people with disabilities can use a place, service or product
reasonable adjustment = a practical change an employer or school must make so a disabled person can take part
wheelchair access = the possibility for a wheelchair user to enter and move around a place
sign language = a visual language using hands, face and body, used by many deaf people
visually impaired = having little or no sight
hearing impairment = partial or complete loss of hearing
learning disability = a reduced ability to understand new or complex information and to learn new skills
neurodiversity = the idea that brains differ and that autism, ADHD and similar conditions are variations, not only defects
mobility aid = a device such as a stick, frame or wheelchair that helps a person move
guide dog = a trained dog that helps a blind or visually impaired person travel safely
Braille = a system of raised dots that blind people read by touch
carer = a person who looks after someone ill, elderly or disabled, often unpaid
long-term care = ongoing help with daily life for people who cannot live fully independently
step-free access = a route into a building or vehicle that does not require climbing steps
first aid = simple medical help given before professional care arrives
recovery position = lying someone on their side so the airway stays open if they are unconscious but breathing
CPR = chest compressions, and sometimes rescue breaths, to keep blood moving when the heart has stopped
defibrillator = a device that can restart the heart with a controlled electric shock
abdominal thrusts = inward and upward presses on the upper abdomen to clear a blocked airway
triage = sorting patients so the most urgent cases are treated first
medical emergency = a sudden, serious health event that needs immediate professional help
emergency services = organisations such as ambulance, fire and police that respond to urgent incidents
adrenaline auto-injector = a device a person at risk of anaphylaxis can use to inject adrenaline quickly
blood donation = giving your blood so it can be used for patients who need it
donor card = a document showing you agree that your organs may be used after death
euthanasia = intentionally ending a person’s life to relieve suffering from a terminal illness, illegal in many countries
medical certificate = an official note from a doctor confirming illness or fitness
vital signs = basic measurements such as pulse, temperature, breathing rate and blood pressure
